title.en: Getting ready for the class party

text.en: The children of Class 3 are getting ready for a party. They decorate the board with paper strings, measure a window and a table, and make costumes for a drama. They find out how to measure length with a hand span, a footstep, a pencil and a string and why a common unit is useful.

We can measure length with parts of our body. A hand span, a footstep and an arm are body units that everyone has. Leena and Adi measure the same table with their hand spans, but they may get different numbers, because their hands are of different sizes. Paper strings, pencils and ropes can also be used as units. When two people use the same unit, they get the same count. To say whether a string is longer or shorter, we put them side by side starting from the same point. The shortest string is the one that ends first and the longest string ends last.
Shelly and Adi want to know if a large table will pass through the door. They cannot lift the table, so they cut a thread as long as the table's breadth and check it against the door. If a thread matches the length of something, we can carry the thread to the other object. A thread is a tool for comparing things that cannot be placed side by side. If both the length and the breadth of a table are more than the width of the door, we may still be able to tilt it through the door, but if the table is too wide it cannot go through. Comparing with a common unit, such as a thread, is called indirect measurement.
Small units such as a pencil are slow to measure a long thing like a saree. A paper strip double the size of a pencil helps, and longer strips help even more. A shopkeeper measures cloth with a metre rod. A metre is a standard unit for length, and it is the same for everyone everywhere. We can make a metre rope. We take a metre rod and a rope, make a knot at one end and another knot at one metre. The length between the knots is a metre. Fold the rope in half to get half a metre and fold again to get a quarter metre. Four quarter metres make a metre and two half metres make a metre. Many children are taller than one metre. Some things in a class are more than a metre long, some less and some about equal to a metre.
Is everyone's head 3 hand spans round, and is a forearm as long as a foot? We can measure and see that these are not exactly true for every child. Before we measure, we estimate. After we measure with the metre rope, we see whose estimate was closest. If we cut a metre rope into 4 equal pieces, we need to make 3 cuts. We can fit a number of footsteps in a metre, and it depends on the size of the feet.

The class needs a strip across a table. One pupil counts six large hand spans and another counts eight small ones. Did the length of the table change?

board.text: Same table: 6 large spans or 8 small spans

text.en: The table is the same length. A smaller unit covers less space per span, so we need more spans to cover the whole table.
Try the same job with identical paper strips. Put the first strip at the edge, then lay each new strip where the last one ends.
A gap leaves out part of the table and an overlap measures a part twice. Place the strips end to end and count only after lining them up.
If four strips fit and the end falls before the fifth strip is complete, the table is more than four strips long and less than five.
You want a ribbon as wide as the noticeboard, but the ribbon is across the room. Use an unmarked thread to carry the width from the board to the ribbon.
Hold the thread straight without stretching it, then compare it with the ribbon from the same starting point. Check whether the ribbon reaches the thread's end.
The same method can help an adult check a table against a door. Measure the clear space between the doorposts, because that is the space the table must pass through.

board.text: Check the clear doorway with an adult

text.en: With a metre rope, line up the first knot with the edge. The second knot marks one metre. Use the knots rather than any extra loose rope outside them.
Mark the middle by folding the metre rope so the knots meet. Open it and lay one half next to a quarter. What total length do you have?
A half can be divided into two quarters. Add one more quarter and you have three quarters of a metre.
Estimate whether the classroom board is shorter than a metre or longer. Check with the metre rope. If it is longer, mark where the first metre ends before moving the rope.
Then place the first knot on that mark and keep going. Moving the same unit with no gaps or overlaps lets you measure a length bigger than your measuring tool.

problem.en: Why do Leena and Adi get different numbers when they measure the same table with their hand spans?

text.en: Hand spans are different sizes.

why.en: Body units differ from person to person.

text.en: A bigger hand span covers more, so Adi counts fewer.

why.en: The count depends on the unit.

text.en: To get the same answer, both should use a standard unit, like a metre or a common strip.

why.en: Everyone then gets the same result.

problem.en: How do you make a half-metre rope from a metre rope?

text.en: Fold the one-metre rope so that the two ends meet.
Each part is half a metre.

why.en: Fold again to get quarter metres.

text.en: Two half-metre ropes make a metre.

problem.en: A metre rope is cut into 4 equal pieces. How many cuts are needed?

text.en: Draw the rope and mark the pieces.
To make 2 pieces we need 1 cut, for 3 pieces 2 cuts, for 4 pieces 3 cuts.

why.en: Pieces are one more than the cuts.

text.en: 3 cuts are needed.

why.en: Each piece is a quarter metre.

prompt.en: Explain why we use a metre to measure instead of a hand span.

requiredIdeas.en: A metre is the same for everyone
A metre helps in measuring long things

commonMisconceptions.en: Everyone has the same hand span

points.en: We can measure length with a hand span, a footstep or a string, but body units differ from person to person.
Comparing with a thread or strip lets us measure indirectly.
A metre is a standard unit of length.
Half a metre and a quarter of a metre can be made by folding a metre rope.
We estimate first and then check by measuring.
